nodes.description: Although impaired TPI activity does not, at the system level, abolish energy metabolism, it causes accumulation of dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) proximal to the enzymatic block. DHAP is chemically converted to the highly reactive dicarbonyl methylglyoxal, which in turn drives the formation of advanced glycation end products. This toxic-metabolite mechanism is the disease-specific arm that distinguishes TPI deficiency from other glycolytic enzymopathies and is implicated in its progressive neurodegeneration.

This arm sets TPI deficiency apart from all other glycolytic enzymopathies.

nodes.description: Biallelic pathogenic variants in TPI1 reduce the activity of triosephosphate isomerase, the enzyme that equilibrates the triose phosphates (dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate) produced by aldolase in glycolysis. The enzyme is catalytically active only as a homodimer; the disease-causing mutations decrease catalytic activity and/or cause dissociation of the dimer into inactive monomers, rather than acting as simple null alleles. The recurrent Glu104Asp (E104D) missense substitution is by far the most common allele. This is the systemic root lesion of the disorder, feeding both a distinctive neurotoxic (methylglyoxal) arm and the erythrocyte glycolytic-failure arm of the conserved hemolytic-anemia module.
